transitivity: both — transitive (work long hours), intransitive (she works downtown)
gloss: To do a job, especially one you are paid for.
examples: I *work* for a small firm downtown.
She *worked* late three nights in a row.
He has been *working* here since 2019.
contrast: Work FOR a company, work AT a place, work ON a project, work WITH people. The preposition changes the meaning, not the verb.

gloss: To pay someone to work for you.
examples: The plant *employs* about two hundred people.
They *employed* him as a night manager.
She has been *employed* by the same firm for ten years.
contrast: The -y follows a vowel, so nothing changes: employs, employed. Compare carry - carries - carried.

gloss: To give someone a job.
examples: We *hire* new engineers every spring.
They *hired* her on the spot.
The company is *hiring* two more designers.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: hiring, not hireing. Hire sounds exactly like higher.

transitivity: both — transitive (recruit engineers), intransitive (we are recruiting again)
gloss: To find and bring in new people to work for an organization.
examples: Big banks *recruit* heavily on college campuses.
We *recruited* four analysts last quarter.
They are *recruiting* for a new sales team.

transitivity: both — transitive (interview five candidates), intransitive (interview for a job)
gloss: To ask someone questions formally, especially to decide whether to give them a job.
examples: The manager *interviews* every finalist himself.
They *interviewed* six people for the position.
I am *interviewing* with two companies this week.

transitivity: both — transitive (train new hires), intransitive (he trained as a nurse)
gloss: To teach someone the skills a job needs.
examples: We *train* every new hire for two weeks.
She *trained* as an accountant before switching to law.
He has *trained* most of the staff on the new system.

transitivity: both — transitive (manage a team), intransitive (somehow we managed)
gloss: To be in charge of a business, a team, or a difficult situation.
examples: She *manages* a team of twelve.
He *managed* the store for eight years.
Who is *managing* the project while you are away?

gloss: To watch over people or work and make sure it is done properly.
examples: Two engineers *supervise* the night shift.
She *supervised* the move to the new office.
The interns are *supervised* by a senior developer.

gloss: To move someone into a higher position, or to help a product become better known.
examples: Good managers *promote* from within.
They *promoted* her to regional director.
He has been *promoted* twice in three years.

transitivity: both — transitive (resign his post), intransitive (she resigned in May)
gloss: To officially leave a job or position.
examples: Two board members *resign* every year by rotation.
He *resigned* after the merger was announced.
She is *resigning* at the end of the month.
contrast: The g is silent: ri-ZYN. You resign FROM a company. Re-sign, meaning to sign again, is a different word: ree-SYN.

gloss: To make someone leave their job, usually for poor work or bad behavior.
examples: No boss enjoys having to *fire* anyone.
They *fired* him for missing three deadlines.
Two people were *fired* after the audit.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: firing. Fire is blunt; let go and dismiss are the polite versions.

gloss: To remove someone from a job, or to refuse to take an idea seriously.
examples: The company rarely *dismisses* anyone without a warning.
She *dismissed* the proposal in one sentence.
He was *dismissed* for gross misconduct.
contrast: After -ss the third person adds -es: dismisses.

gloss: To put a new person or thing in the place of another.
examples: We *replace* the laptops every four years.
She *replaced* the retiring director in June.
Who is *replacing* him while he is on leave?
contrast: Replace X WITH Y, not replace X on Y.

transitivity: both — transitive (transfer the funds), intransitive (she transferred to Dallas)
gloss: To move a person, some money, or a thing from one place or job to another.
examples: We *transfer* the payroll every second Friday.
He *transferred* to the Chicago office last year.
The files are being *transferred* to the new server.
contrast: Stress is on the last syllable, so the r doubles: transferred, transferring. The noun is stressed at the front: TRANS-fur.

transitivity: both — transitive (relocate the plant), intransitive (they relocated to Texas)
gloss: To move a business, a job, or yourself to a different place.
examples: Many firms *relocate* to cut costs.
They *relocated* the whole department to Austin.
She is *relocating* for a better position.

ru: ездить на работу и обратно, добираться до работы
gloss: To travel regularly between your home and your workplace.
examples: I *commute* forty minutes each way.
He *commuted* by train for years.
She is tired of *commuting* into the city.

gloss: To get money for work you do, or to deserve something through effort.
examples: Engineers here *earn* well above the average.
She *earned* a bonus for closing the deal.
He has *earned* the trust of the whole team.

gloss: To plan and arrange something, or to put things in order.
examples: She *organizes* the annual sales meeting.
They *organized* the files by client.
We are *organizing* a training day for June.
contrast: American spelling -ize: organize, organized. British writing uses -ise: organise, organised.

gloss: To make the plans that are needed for something to happen.
examples: I will *arrange* a call for Thursday.
She *arranged* the whole trip in one afternoon.
Transportation has already been *arranged*.

transitivity: both — transitive (coordinate the launch), intransitive (coordinate with the vendor)
gloss: To make different people or parts of a job work together smoothly.
examples: She *coordinates* the work of four teams.
We *coordinated* the launch with the marketing department.
He is *coordinating* the move to the new building.

transitivity: both — transitive (delegate the task), intransitive (good managers delegate)
gloss: To give part of your work or authority to someone else.
examples: Strong managers *delegate* instead of doing everything themselves.
He *delegated* the reporting to his assistant.
By *delegating* the paperwork, she freed up two days a week.
contrast: The verb ends in -gayt; the noun, a person sent to a conference, ends in a schwa: DEL-uh-guht.

gloss: To give a person a particular job, task, or place.
examples: They *assign* each new hire a mentor.
She *assigned* the audit to two junior staff.
I have been *assigned* to the Boston account.
contrast: The g is silent: uh-SYN. Assign a task TO someone.

ru: расставлять приоритеты, ставить на первое место
transitivity: both — transitive (prioritize the bug fixes), intransitive (learn to prioritize)
gloss: To decide which things matter most and deal with them first.
examples: Good teams *prioritize* ruthlessly.
We *prioritized* the three biggest accounts.
He is *prioritizing* safety over speed.

gloss: To give out money, time, or resources for a particular purpose.
examples: The board *allocates* the budget every October.
They *allocated* two engineers to the project.
Half the funds have already been *allocated*.

gloss: To deal with a job, a problem, or a person successfully.
examples: She *handles* all the contracts herself.
He *handled* the complaint calmly.
Who is *handling* the Miller account now?

transitivity: both — transitive (operate the machinery), intransitive (the firm operates in six states)
gloss: To run a business or a machine, or to be active and working.
examples: The company *operates* in twelve countries.
He *operated* a small repair shop for years.
The plant has been *operating* at half capacity.

gloss: To keep something in good condition or at the same level.
examples: We *maintain* records for seven years.
They *maintained* production right through the strike.
The equipment is *maintained* twice a year.

gloss: To make someone want to work hard or to do something.
examples: Money alone does not *motivate* people.
Her speech *motivated* the whole team.
He is very good at *motivating* new staff.

gloss: To give someone the confidence or the reason to do something.
examples: We *encourage* everyone to ask questions.
My manager *encouraged* me to apply.
Staff are *encouraged* to work from home on Fridays.
contrast: Encourage SOMEONE TO DO something: the person and the to-infinitive are both required.

transitivity: both — transitive (focus your attention), intransitive (focus on the deadline)
gloss: To give all your attention to one thing.
examples: Let us *focus* on next quarter.
The team *focused* on cutting costs.
She has been *focusing* on the biggest clients.
contrast: American English keeps one s: focused, focusing. British writing often doubles it: focussed. You focus ON something.

gloss: To plan that something will happen at a particular time.
examples: We *schedule* performance reviews for every March.
She *scheduled* the call for nine in the morning.
The meeting has been *scheduled* twice and canceled twice.
contrast: Americans say SKEJ-ool; the British say SHED-yool. Same spelling, different sound.

gloss: To change something to a different time.
examples: Can we *reschedule* for Friday?
They *rescheduled* the interview twice.
The flight was *rescheduled* for the next morning.

ru: откладывать, отложить; переносить на более поздний срок
gloss: To move an event or a decision to a later time.
examples: Let us not *postpone* the decision again.
They *postponed* the launch until spring.
The hearing has been *postponed* indefinitely.

transitivity: both — transitive (delay the shipment), intransitive (do not delay)
gloss: To make something happen later than planned, or to be slow to act.
examples: Bad weather often *delays* deliveries.
The strike *delayed* the whole project by a month.
Our flight has been *delayed* again.
contrast: The -y follows a vowel, so it stays: delays, delayed. Compare carry - carries - carried.

gloss: To decide that a planned event or arrangement will not happen.
examples: They *cancel* the class if fewer than five people sign up.
She *canceled* the order an hour later.
Two flights have been *canceled* this morning.
contrast: American English keeps one l: canceled, canceling. British English doubles it: cancelled. The noun cancellation has two l's everywhere.

gloss: To say or show that something is definitely true or definitely arranged.
examples: Please *confirm* the meeting by email.
He *confirmed* the price in writing.
Your booking has been *confirmed*.

transitivity: both — transitive (register a company), intransitive (register for the course)
gloss: To put a name or a fact on an official list.
examples: You *register* the business with the state.
She *registered* for the conference in January.
Over four hundred people have *registered*.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so nothing doubles: registered, registering. You register FOR a course.

gloss: To be the person or organization that holds an event and receives the guests.
examples: Our office *hosts* the regional meeting every fall.
They *hosted* a dinner for the visiting clients.
She is *hosting* the webinar on Thursday.

gloss: To arrange in advance to have a room, a seat, or a service.
examples: I always *book* the aisle seat.
She *booked* the conference room for two hours.
The hotel is fully *booked* that week.

transitivity: both — transitive (report the results), intransitive (she reports to the CFO)
gloss: To give an official account of something, or to work directly under someone.
examples: All four managers *report* to her.
He *reported* the problem to security the same day.
Sales figures are *reported* every Monday morning.
contrast: Report TO a person, your boss; report ON a subject.

gloss: To show or explain something formally to a group of people.
examples: I *present* the numbers at every board meeting.
She *presented* the plan to the client on Tuesday.
He is *presenting* at the conference next week.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, pri-ZENT; the noun and adjective on the first, PREZ-unt.

gloss: To write something down or store it so that it can be used later.
examples: We *record* every call for training.
She *recorded* the vote in the minutes.
The session was *recorded* and shared with the team.
contrast: The verb is ri-KORD; the noun is REK-urd, as in a sales record.

gloss: To make something current, or to tell someone the latest news.
examples: Please *update* me before the call.
They *updated* the forecast after the holidays.
The policy was *updated* in January.
contrast: The verb is stressed at the end, up-DAYT; the noun at the front, UP-dayt, as in a quick update.

gloss: To give the main points of something in a short form.
examples: Can you *summarize* the report in one page?
She *summarized* the meeting in three bullet points.
The findings are *summarized* on the last slide.
contrast: American -ize, British -ise: summarize, summarise.

gloss: To examine something carefully in order to understand it.
examples: We *analyze* the sales data every month.
They *analyzed* five years of customer complaints.
The results are still being *analyzed*.
contrast: American analyze, British analyse. Unlike advise, this verb really does change its spelling.

transitivity: both — transitive (research the market), intransitive (research into the causes)
gloss: To study a subject carefully in order to find out new facts.
examples: Our team *researches* the competition before every bid.
She *researched* the market for six months.
He is *researching* new suppliers in Mexico.
contrast: After -ch the third person adds -es: researches.

gloss: To watch and check something regularly over a period of time.
examples: We *monitor* response times around the clock.
They *monitored* the pilot program for a year.
Costs are being *monitored* closely.

gloss: To judge carefully how good or how useful something is.
examples: We *evaluate* every vendor before signing.
They *evaluated* three different systems.
The pilot is still being *evaluated*.

gloss: To judge the amount, value, or quality of something.
examples: Managers *assess* their teams twice a year.
The insurer *assessed* the damage at nine thousand dollars.
We are *assessing* whether the plan is realistic.
contrast: After -ss the third person adds -es: assesses.

gloss: To find the size, amount, or degree of something.
examples: How do you *measure* success here?
They *measured* the impact of the ad campaign.
Performance is *measured* against last year.

gloss: To look at something again carefully in order to judge or change it.
examples: We *review* salaries in December.
She *reviewed* the contract line by line.
Your application is being *reviewed*.

gloss: To say roughly how much or how many, without measuring exactly.
examples: Contractors usually *estimate* high.
They *estimated* the repair at two thousand dollars.
Delivery is *estimated* at four to six weeks.
contrast: The verb ends in -mayt; the noun ends in a schwa: ES-tuh-mut, a written estimate.

gloss: To work out an amount or a number using arithmetic.
examples: The system *calculates* overtime automatically.
She *calculated* the shipping costs by hand.
Interest is *calculated* monthly.

gloss: To check that something is true or accurate.
examples: We *verify* every invoice before payment.
She *verified* his references by phone.
The figures have been *verified* by an outside auditor.
contrast: Consonant plus -y changes to -ies and -ied: verifies, verified. But verifying keeps the y.

gloss: To follow the progress or the position of something over time.
examples: We *track* every order from the warehouse to the door.
They *tracked* expenses in a simple spreadsheet.
Your package is being *tracked*.

transitivity: both — transitive (negotiate a contract), intransitive (negotiate with the union)
gloss: To discuss something formally in order to reach an agreement.
examples: We *negotiate* the terms before signing anything.
She *negotiated* a ten percent discount.
They are still *negotiating* with the supplier.
contrast: The -ti- sounds like sh: ni-GOH-shee-ayt. Negotiate WITH someone, OVER a price.

ru: идти на компромисс, договариваться; ставить под угрозу
transitivity: both — transitive (compromise the deal), intransitive (both sides compromised)
gloss: To settle an argument by each side giving up part of what it wants.
examples: Neither side wants to *compromise*.
They *compromised* on a two-year contract.
By *compromising* early, we saved a month of argument.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, and the ending sounds like -myz, not -mees.

gloss: To suggest a plan or an idea formally.
examples: I *propose* that we push the launch to May.
She *proposed* a simpler pricing model.
The changes *proposed* last week were approved.

gloss: To put forward an idea for someone to think about.
examples: Let me *suggest* another approach.
He *suggested* moving the meeting to Friday.
It has been *suggested* that we hire a consultant.
contrast: No indirect object: suggest something TO someone, or suggest doing something. Never suggest me to do it.

gloss: To tell someone that a person or a thing is good or right for a purpose.
examples: I *recommend* the shorter contract.
She *recommended* him for the promotion.
This supplier was *recommended* by our lawyer.
contrast: One c, two m's: re-comm-end. Like suggest, it takes recommend that we do or recommend doing, not recommend me to do.

gloss: To tell someone what you think they should do.
examples: Our lawyers *advise* us to wait.
She *advised* him against taking the offer.
We were *advised* to keep the receipts.
contrast: Advise is the verb and ends in a z sound; advice is the noun and ends in s. Both keep -ise in American English.

gloss: To say that you are willing to give or to do something.
examples: They *offer* a discount for early payment.
The company *offered* her the job on Friday.
He has been *offered* a transfer to Denver.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the r does not double: offered, offering.

gloss: To agree to take something that is offered.
examples: We *accept* purchase orders by email.
She *accepted* the offer the next morning.
His resignation has been *accepted*.
contrast: Do not confuse accept, to take, with except, apart from. They sound almost the same.

gloss: To refuse to accept an offer, an idea, or an application.
examples: The bank *rejects* about half of these applications.
They *rejected* our first bid.
The proposal was *rejected* without discussion.
contrast: The verb is stressed at the end, ri-JEKT; the noun, a faulty item, at the front: REE-jekt.

transitivity: both — transitive (decline the invitation), intransitive (sales declined)
gloss: To politely refuse something, or to go down in amount or quality.
examples: I have to *decline* the invitation.
Profits *declined* for three quarters in a row.
She has *declined* two offers this year.

transitivity: both — transitive (refuse the offer), intransitive (he simply refused)
gloss: To say firmly that you will not do or accept something.
examples: They *refuse* to negotiate before Monday.
He *refused* to sign the new terms.
Our claim has been *refused* twice.
contrast: The verb is ri-FYOOZ; the noun refuse, meaning garbage, is REF-yooss.

gloss: To ask for something politely or formally.
examples: Employees *request* time off through the portal.
She *requested* a copy of the contract.
The documents you *requested* are attached.

gloss: To need something, or to make something a rule.
examples: The job *requires* three years of experience.
They *required* two forms of identification.
A signature is *required* on every page.

gloss: To ask for something forcefully, as if you have a right to it.
examples: The workers *demand* a written contract.
She *demanded* an explanation from the vendor.
A refund was *demanded* within the hour.
contrast: American /æ/: di-MAND, not di-MAHND.

transitivity: both — transitive (settle the dispute), intransitive (the two sides settled)
gloss: To end an argument or a debt by agreement.
examples: Most cases like this *settle* before trial.
They *settled* the claim out of court.
The invoice has been *settled* in full.

gloss: To put something into its final, agreed form.
examples: We *finalize* the budget in November.
They *finalized* the deal on Friday afternoon.
The wording is still being *finalized*.

gloss: To write a first version of a document.
examples: Legal will *draft* the agreement.
She *drafted* the email but never sent it.
A new policy is being *drafted*.
contrast: American /æ/: DRAFT, not DRAHFT.

gloss: To change a document, a plan, or a figure after looking at it again.
examples: We *revise* the forecast every quarter.
He *revised* the proposal after her comments.
These are the *revised* numbers.
contrast: In American English revise means to rewrite or correct. It does not mean to study for an exam, which is the usual British sense.

gloss: To make an agreement, a license, or a subscription valid for another period.
examples: We *renew* the lease every two years.
She *renewed* her contract for another term.
The license has not been *renewed*.
contrast: American ri-NOO, not ri-NYOO.

gloss: To make something last longer or reach further.
examples: Can you *extend* the deadline by a week?
They *extended* his contract through December.
The warranty has been *extended* to three years.

gloss: To tell people about something publicly and officially.
examples: The chief executive *announces* the results on Tuesday.
They *announced* the merger before the market opened.
A new director has been *announced*.

gloss: To tell someone about something officially.
examples: We *inform* clients of any price change in writing.
She *informed* human resources the same day.
Staff were *informed* by email on Monday.
contrast: Inform SOMEONE of or about something: the person comes first.

gloss: To tell someone officially, usually in advance.
examples: The system *notifies* the manager automatically.
They *notified* us two weeks before the change.
You will be *notified* by email.
contrast: Consonant plus -y changes: notifies, notified. Notifying keeps the y.

gloss: To answer someone, especially in writing.
examples: She always *replies* within a day.
He *replied* to my message that evening.
Nobody has *replied* to the invitation yet.
contrast: Reply TO a person or a message, never reply me. Consonant plus -y: replies, replied.

ru: писать по электронной почте, отправлять письмо по электронной почте
gloss: To send someone a message by electronic mail.
examples: I *email* the report every Friday.
She *emailed* me the invoice this morning.
The schedule has been *emailed* to everyone.

gloss: To act or to speak officially for a person, a group, or a company.
examples: Two lawyers *represent* the company in court.
She *represented* us at the trade show.
The union is *representing* the night shift.

gloss: To give official permission for something.
examples: Only two people *authorize* payments over ten thousand dollars.
She *authorized* the overtime herself.
The purchase was never *authorized*.
contrast: American -ize, British -ise: authorize, authorise.

gloss: To allow something officially.
examples: The rules do not *permit* outside contractors on site.
They *permitted* us to use the loading dock.
Smoking is not *permitted* anywhere in the building.
contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the t doubles: permitted, permitting. The noun, a document, is stressed at the front: PUR-mit.

gloss: To choose someone officially for a job or a position.
examples: The board *appoints* the chief executive.
They *appointed* her head of operations.
A new auditor has been *appointed*.

gloss: To start something new, especially a product or a campaign.
examples: We *launch* the new version in March.
They *launched* the app without any advertising.
The campaign is being *launched* in three cities.
contrast: After -ch the third person adds -es: launches.

transitivity: both — transitive (develop a product), intransitive (the market developed quickly)
gloss: To create something over time, or to grow and become more advanced.
examples: Our team *develops* software for hospitals.
They *developed* the prototype in four months.
We are *developing* a cheaper version.
contrast: No doubled p and no final e: developed, developing, development.

gloss: To plan how something will look or work before it is made.
examples: She *designs* packaging for food brands.
They *designed* the store layout themselves.
The system was *designed* for small teams.
contrast: The g is silent: di-ZYN. It comes back in designate and designation.

gloss: To make or grow something, especially in large amounts.
examples: The plant *produces* four thousand units a day.
They *produced* the entire run in Mexico.
Most of our parts are *produced* locally.
contrast: The verb is pruh-DOOSS; the noun produce, meaning fruit and vegetables, is PROH-dooss.

gloss: To make goods in a factory, usually in large quantities.
examples: They *manufacture* medical equipment in Ohio.
These chips were *manufactured* in Taiwan.
The company has been *manufacturing* here since 1962.

gloss: To advertise and sell a product to a particular group of buyers.
examples: They *market* the service to small businesses.
The drink was *marketed* as a health product.
We are *marketing* it mainly through social media.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the t does not double: marketed, marketing.

transitivity: both — transitive (advertise the position), intransitive (we advertise on the radio)
gloss: To tell the public about a product, a service, or a job.
examples: We *advertise* openings on three job boards.
They *advertised* the sale for two weeks.
The job was never *advertised* publicly.
contrast: Always -ise, in America too: advertise, never advertize. Compare organize and analyze, which do change.

gloss: To provide someone with something they need, especially goods.
examples: Two farms *supply* all of our produce.
They *supplied* the parts at cost.
The materials are *supplied* by a local firm.
contrast: Consonant plus -y: supplies, supplied, but supplying keeps the y. Supply someone WITH something.

transitivity: both — transitive (deliver the order), intransitive (they deliver on Saturdays)
gloss: To take goods to a place, or to do what you promised.
examples: We *deliver* within two business days.
They *delivered* the shipment a day early.
The results were *delivered* exactly as promised.

gloss: To send goods to a customer or to another place.
examples: We *ship* worldwide from a single warehouse.
They *shipped* the order the same afternoon.
Your package has already been *shipped*.
contrast: One short vowel plus one consonant, so the p doubles: shipped, shipping.

gloss: To ask a company to supply goods, or to tell someone to do something.
examples: We *order* supplies once a month.
She *ordered* fifty chairs for the training room.
The parts were *ordered* in April and arrived in July.

gloss: To buy something, especially in formal or business language.
examples: The city *purchases* its vehicles through a state contract.
They *purchased* the building in 2019.
Equipment *purchased* this year is still under warranty.

gloss: To send someone a statement of how much they owe.
examples: We *bill* clients at the end of the month.
They *billed* us twice for the same visit.
You will be *billed* only after delivery.
contrast: Bill someone FOR something: they billed us for the repair.

gloss: To provide the money for a project or an organization.
examples: Two investors *fund* most of the research.
The state *funded* half the construction.
The program is *funded* through 2027.

ru: планировать бюджет, закладывать в бюджет; выделять средства
transitivity: both — transitive (budget ten thousand dollars), intransitive (budget for repairs)
gloss: To plan how much money you will spend on something.
examples: We *budget* about five percent for training.
They *budgeted* twenty thousand dollars for the move.
Nobody had *budgeted* for a second audit.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the t stays single: budgeted, budgeting. Budget FOR something.

transitivity: both — transitive (expand the range), intransitive (the firm expanded)
gloss: To become larger, or to make something larger.
examples: Small firms *expand* slowly at first.
They *expanded* into Canada last year.
We have been *expanding* the team all spring.

transitivity: both — transitive (merge the two departments), intransitive (the banks merged)
gloss: To join two companies, groups, or things into one.
examples: The two firms plan to *merge* next year.
They *merged* the sales and support teams.
The files have been *merged* into one document.
contrast: Merge WITH another company; merge two things INTO one.

gloss: To buy or obtain something, especially a company, a property, or a skill.
examples: Big platforms *acquire* small startups every month.
They *acquired* the rights for two million dollars.
The company was *acquired* by a German group.

gloss: To start an organization or a system that is meant to last.
examples: New owners usually *establish* their own rules.
They *established* the firm in a garage.
The company was *established* in 1948.
contrast: After -sh the third person adds -es: establishes.

gloss: To start a company, a school, or an organization.
examples: It takes nerve to *found* a company alone.
She *founded* the agency at twenty-six.
The firm was *founded* by two former teachers.
contrast: This is a regular verb: found - founded - founded. Do not confuse it with found, the past of find. He founded the company; he found the keys.

gloss: To have something as your property.
examples: She *owns* two restaurants downtown.
They *owned* the building before the bank took it.
The chain is *owned* by a family in Texas.
contrast: Own describes a state, so it is rarely used in the -ing form: she owns it, not she is owning it.

transitivity: both — transitive (rent an office), intransitive (we rent, we do not own)
gloss: To pay to use a property for a period, or to let someone use yours for payment.
examples: We *rent* the second floor.
They *rented* a warehouse near the airport.
The office has been *rented* to a law firm.
contrast: Rent FROM the owner, rent TO a tenant. American English uses rent for both sides; the British often say let for the owner's side.

transitivity: both — transitive (improve the process), intransitive (results improved)
gloss: To make something better, or to become better.
examples: Small changes *improve* the process a lot.
Delivery times *improved* after the new software.
Service has been *improving* since January.

transitivity: both — transitive (increase the price), intransitive (costs increased)
gloss: To become greater in number or amount, or to make something greater.
examples: We *increase* prices once a year.
Sales *increased* by nine percent.
Rent has *increased* every year since 2020.
contrast: The verb is stressed at the end, in-KREESS; the noun at the front, IN-kreess, as in a pay increase.

gloss: To make something smaller in size, amount, or price.
examples: We need to *reduce* overtime.
They *reduced* the headcount by twenty.
Costs have been *reduced* by a third.
contrast: American ri-DOOSS, not ri-DYOOSS.

gloss: To finish something, or to fill in every part of a form.
examples: Please *complete* the form before Friday.
They *completed* the building two months early.
The training must be *completed* within thirty days.

transitivity: both — transitive (finish the report), intransitive (the meeting finished at five)
gloss: To bring something to an end, or to come to an end.
examples: He usually *finishes* by six.
She *finished* the report on the train.
We are *finishing* the last section today.
contrast: Finish DOING something, never finish to do: I finished writing the report.

gloss: To succeed in reaching a goal after effort.
examples: Few teams *achieve* that in a single quarter.
They *achieved* record sales in December.
Nothing would have been *achieved* without her.
contrast: Spelled -ie-: achieve, achieved, not acheive.

gloss: To finish something successfully, especially something difficult.
examples: Long meetings rarely *accomplish* much.
The team *accomplished* a great deal in six weeks.
We have *accomplished* everything on the list.
contrast: After -sh the third person adds -es: accomplishes.

ru: терпеть неудачу, провалиться; не суметь, не справиться
transitivity: both — transitive (fail the exam), intransitive (the business failed)
gloss: To not succeed, or to not do something that you should have done.
examples: Most new restaurants *fail* in the first year.
The supplier *failed* to deliver on time.
Two of the three pilot projects have *failed*.
contrast: Fail TO DO something: he failed to answer, not he failed answering.

transitivity: both — transitive (serve customers), intransitive (she served on the board)
gloss: To work for a person, an organization, or a group of customers.
examples: One office *serves* the whole region.
He *served* as treasurer for six years.
Over a thousand clients are *served* each month.

gloss: To make someone pleased, or to meet a requirement.
examples: One supplier cannot *satisfy* all of these demands.
The new design *satisfies* every safety rule.
Her answer *satisfied* the auditors completely.
contrast: Consonant plus -y: satisfies, satisfied. Satisfying keeps the y.

gloss: To deal with documents, data, or materials in an official or standard way.
examples: The bank *processes* refunds in five days.
They *processed* my application the same week.
Your order is being *processed*.
contrast: American English stresses the first syllable and uses the LOT vowel: PRAH-sess.

transitivity: both — transitive (file a complaint), intransitive (file for bankruptcy)
gloss: To send an official document to an authority, or to store papers in order.
examples: Most companies *file* their taxes in March.
She *filed* a complaint with the labor board.
The paperwork was *filed* a week late.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: filing. File FOR bankruptcy, file a complaint WITH an office.

gloss: To pay an outside company to do work that your own staff used to do.
examples: Many firms *outsource* payroll.
They *outsourced* customer support to a call center.
Half of our technical work is now *outsourced*.

gloss: To make a process run by machines or software instead of by people.
examples: We *automate* anything we do more than twice.
They *automated* the whole billing cycle.
Most of the reporting is now *automated*.

transitivity: both — transitive (travel the country), intransitive (she travels for work)
gloss: To go from one place to another, especially over a distance.
examples: I *travel* about once a month for work.
She *traveled* to four countries last quarter.
He has been *traveling* since Tuesday.
contrast: American English keeps one l: traveled, traveling, traveler. British English doubles it: travelled, travelling, traveller.

gloss: To give things out to a number of people, or to supply goods to stores.
examples: Two warehouses *distribute* to the whole West Coast.
They *distributed* the agenda before the meeting.
Bonuses are *distributed* in December.

gloss: To make something easier to understand by explaining it more clearly.
examples: Let me *clarify* one point.
She *clarified* the terms in a follow-up email.
The policy has been *clarified* twice and is still confusing.
contrast: Consonant plus -y: clarifies, clarified. Clarifying keeps the y.
